To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the proteome of elutriated human myeloid cells is highly similar to the proteome of arrested cells; 2) arrested cells show arrest-specific changes in protein abundance; 3) arrested cells are poised to re-replicate the genome in G2.
the proteome of cells that are arrested at specific cell cycle phases by different methods is different from the proteome of the same cells that are cycling normally.

a large fraction of protein changes in cells arrested by serum starvation, DNA damage or CDK1 inhibition are not related to cell cycle regulation, and that arrested cells often show unexpected patterns of gene expression and protein abundance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of proteins involved in cell cycle control.
the analysis of protein abundance changes in human leukemia cells during the cell cycle.
the identification and characterization of the proteins involved in the control of cell division in human cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cell cycle is not a single, linear pathway, and that the proteomics data presented here provide a valuable resource to understand cell cycle regulation and the mechanisms by which cells respond to cell cycle arrests.
the proteomic data presented in this study are not representative of the physiological cell cycle, but rather reflect the responses of the cells to the different arrest conditions used.
the proteomic analysis of the cell cycle response in the human myeloid NB4 leukemia cell line has been carried out.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the proteome of cells arrested by serum starvation is very similar to the proteome of the G1 phase of the cell cycle, while the proteome of hydroxyurea arrested cells resembles that of the S phase and the proteome of CDK1 inhibited cells resembles that of mitosis.

cell cycle arrests induced by serum starvation, DNA damage and CDK1 inhibition are associated with large-scale changes in protein abundance that are distinct from those observed during normal cell cycle progression.
the proteome of cells arrested in a particular cell cycle phase is not necessarily representative of the proteome of cycling cells at that cell cycle phase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cell cycle is a complex and dynamic process, with a large fraction of its regulation occurring in a phase-dependent manner, rather than in a cell cycle phase-independent manner.

the proteome changes observed across the unperturbed cell cycle are not a reflection of cell cycle progression per se, but rather of the physiological response to cell cycle progression, and thus are not representative of the proteome of a ‘pure’ cell cycle phase.
the proteome of a cell is a dynamic entity that changes in response to a wide range of stimuli.
